title: Heights and Distances
summary: Applied trigonometry: angles of elevation and depression, the 30-45-60 rules, two-angle configurations, moving observers and compound figures. Every question reduces to one right triangle and one tangent — learn the three standard-angle multipliers and the cot-difference formula and this becomes near-guaranteed marks.

subtopics.title: Angles of elevation and depression
subtopics.concept:
Elevation means looking **up** at an angle. Depression means looking **down**. Both angles sit between the **horizontal line** through the observer's eye and the line of sight.

Each question hides one right triangle. The tower is the side opposite the angle. The ground distance is the side next to it. So one ratio, $\tan\theta$, solves most of them.

First turn every depression into an elevation. Then solve the triangle.

formulas.name: Tangent rule
formulas.note: The angle sits at the observer. Height is opposite, distance is next to the angle.

formulas.name: Slanting length (thread, wire, ladder)
formulas.note: L is the slanting line of sight, the hypotenuse of the triangle.

formulas.name: Depression to elevation
formulas.note: The two horizontal lines are parallel, so the angles are equal.

tricks.title: Swap depression for elevation first
tricks.body: Never work with a downward angle directly. Redraw it at the bottom of the tower and solve an ordinary elevation question.

steps: Depression $60^\circ$ means the car sees the top at $60^\circ$.

tricks.body: Whenever the angle is $45^\circ$, the height above the eye equals the horizontal distance. Write the equal pair without any tangent.

mistakes.right: The angle is at the observer, the tower is opposite it, so use $\tan\theta$.

mistakes.wrong: Measuring the angle of depression from the vertical line downward.
mistakes.right: Depression is measured from the horizontal line through the eye, going down.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the kite thread or ladder length as the height.
mistakes.right: The thread is the hypotenuse: height $= L\sin\theta$, distance $= L\cos\theta$.

mistakes.right: Add the eye height to the height above the eye at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Turning a depression into an elevation and then changing its value.
mistakes.right: The two angles are equal. Only the position of the angle moves.

subtopics.notes:
### Looking up: the angle of elevation
Stand on flat ground and look straight ahead. Now raise your eyes to the top of a tower.

The angle your line of sight turns **up** from the horizontal is the **angle of elevation**.

The horizontal ray and the tower make a right angle. So the figure is a right triangle:

- Tower = the side **opposite** the angle.
- Ground distance = the side **next to** the angle.
- Eye level = the height of the observer's eye above the ground.

> **Rule:** $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height above eye level}}{\text{horizontal distance}}$

A tower top is seen at $45^\circ$ from a point on the ground. $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so the tower is as tall as the point is far: tower 20 m, distance 20 m.

### Looking down: the angle of depression
Now stand on the tower and look at a car on the road.

The angle your line of sight turns **down** from your horizontal line is the **angle of depression**.

> **Rule:** Depression from the top equals elevation from the bottom. The two horizontal lines are parallel, so the two angles are equal (alternate angles).

This one line converts every depression question into the elevation question you already know.

> **Example:** From the top of a 60 m tower, the angle of depression of a car is $45^\circ$. Then the car sees the tower top at $45^\circ$, so the car is $60 \times \cot 45^\circ = 60$ m from the foot.

### Solve the triangle with tan
Write the ratio before touching any number.

$$h = d \times \tan\theta \qquad d = h \times \cot\theta$$

Here $h$ is the height **above the observer's eye** and $d$ is the horizontal distance.

From a point 30 m from the foot of a pole, its top is at $30^\circ$. Height $= 30 \times \tan 30^\circ = 30 \times \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 10\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Tip:** Keep $\sqrt{3}$ as $\sqrt{3}$ until the last step. Only use $1.73$ when the question says "approximately".

### When the slanting length is given
A kite thread, a wire or a ladder runs **along the line of sight**. That slanting line is the hypotenuse.

- Height reached: $h = L\sin\theta$.
- Horizontal distance: $d = L\cos\theta$.

A kite flies on a 100 m thread at $30^\circ$. Height $= 100 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 50$ m. Horizontal distance $= 100 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 50\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Watch:** The thread is the slanting side, not the height. Options that treat the thread as the height are always present.

### Shadows: similar triangles
The sun makes the same angle with every vertical object at the same time. So the two triangles are similar, and you can compare without trigonometry:

$$\dfrac{\text{tower height}}{\text{tower shadow}} = \dfrac{\text{stick height}}{\text{stick shadow}}$$

A 1.5 m stick casts a 2.5 m shadow. A tower casts a 75 m shadow at the same moment. Tower $= 75 \times \dfrac{1.5}{2.5} = 45$ m.

### Eye level matters
Every angle starts at the observer's **eye**, not the ground.

An observer 1.5 m tall sees a tower top at $45^\circ$ from 20 m away. Height above eye level $= 20$ m. Tower $= 20 + 1.5 = 21.5$ m.

> **Watch:** When the question gives a man's height, add it at the end. When it says "from a point on the ground", the eye is at ground level and nothing is added.

revision: Elevation: angle up from the horizontal at the observer's eye.
Depression: angle down. It equals the elevation from the object below.
$\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{height above eye}}{\text{distance}}$.
Thread, wire, ladder $= L$: use $h = L\sin\theta$, $d = L\cos\theta$.
Shadows: $\dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{shadow}}$ is the same for all objects at one time.
Height above eye $+$ eye height $=$ full height.

subtopics.title: Standard angles: 30°, 45°, 60°
subtopics.concept:
Almost every exam question uses only $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Learn their tangent values once and most questions become one multiplication.

The cotangent column is the handiest: it turns a height into a distance. At $45^\circ$ the distance equals the height; at $30^\circ$ it is $\sqrt{3}$ times the height; at $60^\circ$ it is $\sqrt{3}$ divided by the height's factor.

formulas.name: Ladder on a wall
formulas.note: Theta is the ladder's angle with the ground.

tricks.title: Read distance straight off the cot column
tricks.body: With a standard angle, distance = height $\times$ the cot value. No division, no fraction juggling.

example.q: A tower 30 m tall has its top seen at $60^\circ$ from a point on the ground. How far is the point from the foot?

tricks.title: Fifteen and seventy-five multiply to one
tricks.body: Angles that add to $90^\circ$ have tangents that multiply to 1. Use this to check answers or flip a division into a multiplication.

mistakes.right: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$; the big value belongs to $60^\circ$.

mistakes.wrong: Computing distance as height $\times\tan\theta$.
mistakes.right: Distance $= h \times \cot\theta$; the tangent gives height from distance.

mistakes.wrong: Using the ladder's length as the height it reaches.
mistakes.right: Height on the wall $= L\sin\theta$; the ladder itself is the slanting side.

mistakes.wrong: Placing the $30^\circ$ ladder angle at the top of the wall.
mistakes.right: The ladder's angle is normally with the ground. At the wall, the angle is $60^\circ$.

mistakes.wrong: Replacing $\sqrt{3}$ by 1.7 in an exact-answer question.
mistakes.right: Keep $\sqrt{3}$ symbolic unless the question says approximately or gives $1.73$.

subtopics.notes:
### The three friendly angles
Exam papers love $30^\circ$, $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ because their ratios are clean.

| Angle | $\tan$ | $\cot$ (distance per unit height) |
|---|---|---|
| $30^\circ$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ | $\sqrt{3}$ |
| $45^\circ$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $60^\circ$ | $\sqrt{3}$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ |

> **Tip:** Memorise the $\cot$ column as "how far you stand from a 1 m object". At $30^\circ$ you stand $\sqrt{3}$ m; at $60^\circ$ only $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ m.

Worked number: a tower is $30\sqrt{3}$ m tall and its top is seen at $30^\circ$. Distance $= 30\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 90$ m.

### Swapping between height and distance
One multiplication is enough, once the angle is standard.

$$d = h \times \cot\theta \qquad h = d \times \tan\theta$$

A point is 90 m from the foot of a tower, and the top is at $60^\circ$. Height $= 90 \times \sqrt{3} = 90\sqrt{3}$ m. Check the size: a near angle ($60^\circ$) with a long distance must give a tall tower.

> **Rule:** Bigger angle, closer point. At $60^\circ$ the tower is about 1.7 times the distance; at $30^\circ$ it is about 0.6 times.

### Spotting the angle from the sides
Sometimes the sides are given and the angle is asked.

A tower 20 m tall casts a shadow 20 m long. Height equals distance, and only one angle makes the legs equal: $45^\circ$.

> **Example:** A tower is $\sqrt{3}$ times as far from you as it is tall, so $\cot\theta = \sqrt{3}$, so $\theta = 30^\circ$.

### Ladders and slanting wires
When the slanting length $L$ is given, use sine and cosine.

A 20 m ladder leans on a wall at $30^\circ$ with the ground:

- Height on the wall $= 20 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 10$ m.
- Foot from the wall $= 20 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Watch:** The $30^\circ$ angle is between the ladder and the **ground**. If it is given at the wall, swap sine and cosine.

### The fifteen and seventy-five pair
Two more exact values appear in harder papers:

$$\tan 75^\circ = 2 + \sqrt{3}, \qquad \tan 15^\circ = 2 - \sqrt{3}$$

They multiply to 1, because $15^\circ + 75^\circ = 90^\circ$.

A tower 10 m tall is seen at $15^\circ$. Distance $= \dfrac{10}{2-\sqrt{3}} = 10(2+\sqrt{3}) = 20 + 10\sqrt{3}$ m. Rationalise by multiplying top and bottom by $2+\sqrt{3}$.

### When the sun moves
As the sun climbs, the shadow shrinks. Two positions of the same shadow give one equation.

A tower's shadow shortens by 10 m as the sun moves from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$:

$$h(\cot 30^\circ - \cot 60^\circ) = 10 \Rightarrow h \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 10 \Rightarrow h = 5\sqrt{3} \text{ m}$$

> **Tip:** For the $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ pair, $\cot 30^\circ - \cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. The same difference appears in many questions.

revision: $\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, $\tan 45^\circ = 1$, $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$.

Ladder: height $= L\sin\theta$, foot distance $= L\cos\theta$.
$\tan 75^\circ = 2+\sqrt{3}$, $\tan 15^\circ = 2-\sqrt{3}$, product $1$.
Shadow change: $h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$ = change in length.

subtopics.title: Two observation points (two angles)
subtopics.concept:
One angle gives only a ratio: two sides, one equation. Two angles from two places give the height itself.

The trick is simple. Write $h\cot\alpha$ for one distance and $h\cot\beta$ for the other. The walked gap between the two viewpoints is the difference (same side) or the sum (opposite sides) of these.

So every two-angle question is one equation with one unknown: $h$.

formulas.name: Same side (walk towards)
formulas.note: d is the distance walked; beta is the nearer, bigger angle.

formulas.name: Opposite sides
formulas.note: d is the full distance between the two observers.

formulas.name: Gap between two objects from a height
Tower seen from foot and roof of a building
formulas.note: b = building height; beta from the foot, alpha from the roof.

tricks.title: Thirty-sixty fast numbers
tricks.body: For the 30 and 60 pair: same side $h = d\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$; opposite sides $h = d\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$. Both come from $\cot 30^\circ - \cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$.

example.q: Walking 20 m towards a tower raises the angle from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height.

tricks.title: Write the cot pair before the numbers
tricks.body: Always simplify $\cot\alpha - \cot\beta$ (or the sum) first. Substituting numbers into unsimplified surds is where errors creep in.

example.q: Two observers 80 m apart on opposite sides see a tower top at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. Find the height.

mistakes.wrong: Using a difference of cotangents for observers on opposite sides.
mistakes.right: Opposite sides add the distances, so use $\cot\alpha+\cot\beta$.

mistakes.wrong: Subtracting the angles first and then taking one cotangent.
mistakes.right: The cotangents subtract, never the angles.

mistakes.wrong: Treating the midpoint between two towers as the full distance to each.
mistakes.right: From the midpoint each tower is half the road away.

mistakes.wrong: Using the far angle as the near one.
mistakes.right: Walking towards the tower raises the angle; the bigger angle is the closer point.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting both triangles share the same tower height.
mistakes.right: Write $h$ once and use it in both cotangent expressions.

subtopics.notes:
### Why two angles are enough
A single angle only tells you a ratio. Add a second viewpoint and the ground between them, and the height falls out.

Set the tower's height as $h$. From point P the angle is $\alpha$, from point Q it is $\beta$. Then:

- Distance of P from the foot $= h\cot\alpha$.
- Distance of Q from the foot $= h\cot\beta$.

Everything else is adding or subtracting these two lengths.

> **Rule:** Same side of the tower: the gap is a **difference**. Opposite sides: the gap is a **sum**.

### Walking towards the tower
The most common pattern. A man sees the top at $30^\circ$, walks some distance towards it, and sees $60^\circ$.

$$h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta) = d \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad h = \frac{d}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$$

The walked distance is 40 m: $h\left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = h \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 40$, so $h = 20\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Tip:** For the $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ pair, $\cot 30^\circ - \cot 60^\circ = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. So $h = d \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$: with $d = 40$, $h = 20\sqrt{3}$ m in one step.

### Watching from opposite sides
Two men stand on opposite banks of a river, or the two angles at the tower top are measured from two sides.

$$h = \frac{d}{\cot\alpha + \cot\beta}$$

Two points are 80 m apart on opposite sides of a tower, with angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$: $h\left(\sqrt{3} + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) = h \times \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}} = 80$, so $h = 20\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Watch:** If a question says "the angles of elevation of the top of an unfinished tower", the taller part still counts: draw the full height in both triangles.

### Two objects seen from a height
From the top of a lighthouse $h$ metres high, two boats lie in the same line, at depressions $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Each boat's distance from the foot is $h\cot\alpha$ and $h\cot\beta$. The distance **between the boats** is:

$$\text{gap} = h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$$

From a 60 m lighthouse the depressions are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$: gap $= 60 \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 40\sqrt{3}$ m.

### Two towers from one point
Two towers stand on opposite sides of a road. From a point on the road, their tops are at $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

Each tower makes its own triangle sharing the same ground distance $d$: heights are $d\tan\alpha$ and $d\tan\beta$.

From the midpoint of a 60 m road, the angles are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. Each tower is 30 m away: heights $= 30\sqrt{3}$ m and $10\sqrt{3}$ m. Difference $= 20\sqrt{3}$ m.

### Watching from two floors
A tower is seen from the foot of a building and again from its roof, $b$ metres higher.

From the foot the angle is $\beta$ (larger). From the roof it is $\alpha$ (smaller), because the roof already covers part of the height. The two equations are $H = d\tan\beta$ and $H - b = d\tan\alpha$. Subtract:

$$d = \frac{b}{\tan\beta - \tan\alpha}, \qquad H = d\tan\beta$$

Building 10 m, roof $30^\circ$, foot $60^\circ$: $d = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{3} - 1/\sqrt{3}} = 5\sqrt{3}$ m and $H = 5\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 15$ m.

> **Watch:** From the higher point the angle is smaller, because the tower top is closer to eye level.

patterns.name: Walking towards the tower
patterns.howToSpot: The angle of elevation increases as the observer walks a given distance towards the tower.
steps: Name the two angles: far first, near second.
Write both distances from the foot: $h\cot\alpha$ and $h\cot\beta$.
Their difference equals the distance walked.
patterns.why: The same height sits inside two triangles, so the walked ground equals the difference of the two cotangent distances.

patterns.howToSpot: From the top of a lighthouse or cliff, two boats or cars are seen at two angles of depression.

Distance of the farther object $= h\cot\alpha$ (smaller angle).
Subtract the nearer distance $h\cot\beta$ to get the gap.
patterns.why: Each object sits at its own cotangent distance from the foot, so the gap is their difference.

patterns.name: Two towers seen from one point
patterns.howToSpot: Two towers on opposite sides of a road; from a point between them both tops are seen.
steps: Split the ground distance as the question directs (midpoint means half each).
Each tower forms its own right triangle.
Compute each height; subtract if a difference is asked.
patterns.why: The triangles are independent, joined only by the shared ground distance.

example.q: Two towers stand on opposite sides of a road 60 m wide. From the midpoint of the road, their tops are seen at $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The difference of their heights is:
steps: Each tower is 30 m from the midpoint.

patterns.name: Tower seen from the foot and the roof of a building
patterns.howToSpot: The same tower's top is observed from ground level and from a window or roof above.
steps: Let the building be $b$ and the tower $H$, with ground distance $d$.
From the foot: $\tan\beta = H/d$. From the roof: $\tan\alpha = (H-b)/d$.
Subtract to eliminate $H$ and find $d$, then $H = d\tan\beta$.
patterns.why: Raising the observer cuts the tower's apparent height by exactly the building's height.

example.q: A tower is seen from the foot of a 10 m building at $60^\circ$, and from its roof at $30^\circ$. The height of the tower is:

revision: Same side: $h = \dfrac{d}{\cot\alpha - \cot\beta}$.
Opposite sides: $h = \dfrac{d}{\cot\alpha + \cot\beta}$.
$30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ pair: difference $= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, sum $= \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{3}}$.
Two boats from a lighthouse: gap $= h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$.
Two towers from a midpoint: each is half the road away; heights $= \dfrac{d}{2}\tan\alpha$ and $\dfrac{d}{2}\tan\beta$.
Foot and roof of a building: $d = \dfrac{b}{\tan\beta - \tan\alpha}$, $H = d\tan\beta$.

subtopics.title: Moving observers: speed and time
subtopics.concept:
A car, a man or a plane moves while someone watches. Motion adds only one new fact: **distance = speed $\times$ time**.

That product replaces the 'walked distance' of the two-angle questions. So the master equation becomes speed $\times$ time $= h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$.

Convert every speed to metres per second first. Then the question is an old friend.

formulas.name: Moving observer chain
formulas.note: alpha = first (farther) angle, beta = second (nearer) angle.

formulas.name: Time to reach the foot
formulas.note: Use the angle at the car's current position.

formulas.name: Vertical rise
formulas.note: d = fixed horizontal distance; angles of depression shrink as the balloon rises.

tricks.title: One chain, any unknown
tricks.body: $v t = h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$ contains every moving-observer question. Cover the unknown and solve.

example.q: A jeep takes 3 s at 8 m/s to change a tower's elevation from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height.

tricks.title: Check the units before the triangle
tricks.body: Convert km/h to m/s with $5/18$ before anything else. A speed in the wrong unit spoils an otherwise perfect triangle.

example.q: A car at 36 km/h takes 10 s to change the elevation from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height.

mistakes.wrong: Using $v\times t$ as the height instead of the ground distance.
mistakes.right: Speed times time is ground covered; it equals the cotangent difference.

mistakes.wrong: Working in km/h with metres in the same equation.
mistakes.right: Convert with $\times\dfrac{5}{18}$ first.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the total time when the remaining time to the foot is asked.
mistakes.right: After the second angle, the car still has $h\cot\beta$ to cover; divide that by the speed.

mistakes.wrong: Adding angles of two observers who move on opposite sides.
mistakes.right: Opposite sides still add the two cotangent distances; only the ground differs.

subtopics.notes:
### Motion only supplies the ground distance
In a moving-observer question, the triangle does not change. Only the ground between the two viewpoints is now covered at a speed.

$$v \times t = h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)$$

Here $v$ is the speed, $t$ the time between the two angle readings, $h$ the tower height, $\alpha$ the first (farther) angle and $\beta$ the second (nearer) angle.

> **Example:** A car running at 6 m/s takes 6 s to change the elevation of a tower top from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Ground covered $= 36$ m. Then $36 = h \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $h = 18\sqrt{3}$ m.

### Finding the height
Given speed, time and both angles, the height comes out in two lines.

1. Ground distance $= v \times t$.
2. Divide by $\cot\alpha - \cot\beta$.

At $4$ m/s for $5$ s the car covers 20 m, so $h = 20 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Tip:** For $30^\circ \to 60^\circ$, $h = (v t)\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. One multiplication, no surd subtraction.

### Finding the speed or the time
The same equation reads in any direction. Solve for what is missing.

A car changes the elevation from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in 5 s, and the tower is known to be $10\sqrt{3}$ m. Ground covered $= h \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 20$ m. Speed $= 20 \div 5 = 4$ m/s.

> **Watch:** Speeds in km/h must be converted: multiply by $\dfrac{5}{18}$ to get m/s. 36 km/h is 10 m/s.

### Time to reach the foot
Sometimes the question asks how much longer the car needs to reach the tower.

After the second reading, the car is still $h\cot\beta$ away (using the **nearer** angle). Divide that distance by the speed.

A tower is $18\sqrt{3}$ m tall and a car sees its top at $30^\circ$. Distance $= 18\sqrt{3} \times \sqrt{3} = 54$ m. At 6 m/s the car needs $54 \div 6 = 9$ s more.

### Moving on both sides
Two friends drive towards the same tower from opposite sides at the same speed.

Each starts at $h\cot\alpha$ or $h\cot\beta$ away. Their arrival times differ by:

$$\Delta t = \frac{h(\cot\alpha - \cot\beta)}{v}$$

Tower $30\sqrt{3}$ m, angles $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$, both at 6 m/s: distances $30$ m and $90$ m, times $5$ s and $15$ s. The nearer starter wins by 10 s.

### Rising straight up
A balloon rises vertically while someone watches a point on the ground. The horizontal distance stays fixed; the height changes.

At horizontal distance $d$: heights are $d\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $d\tan 60^\circ = d\sqrt{3}$. The rise $= d \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$. With $d = 30$ m, the balloon climbed $20\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Rule:** Horizontal motion changes the distance; vertical motion changes the height. Check which one is fixed before writing tan or cot.

subtopics.title: Compound figures: buildings, pedestals, broken objects
subtopics.concept:
Compound figures stack two heights or bend one object: a statue on a pedestal, a tower on a building, a broken tree.

The method never changes. Draw the two triangles separately. The lower triangle gives the ground distance. The upper triangle gives the extra height.

Most answers reduce to one line: extra height $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$.

formulas.note: d comes from the lower triangle: d = pedestal height x cot alpha.

formulas.name: From a roof: depression and elevation
Broken tree

tricks.title: Subtract the tans, multiply once
tricks.body: For any stacked object, extra height $= d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$. Compute the tangent difference first, then one multiplication.

subtopics.notes:
### Two heights stacked
A statue stands on a pedestal. From one point you see the pedestal's top at $\alpha$ and the statue's head at $\beta$.

The lower triangle fixes the ground: $d = p\cot\alpha$, where $p$ is the pedestal's height. The statue's height is then:

$$s = d(\tan\beta - \tan\alpha)$$

Pedestal 30 m, angles $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$: $d = 30$, and $s = 30(\sqrt{3} - 1) = 30\sqrt{3} - 30$ m.

> **Rule:** The difference of tangents times the ground distance gives the stacked part. Never multiply the whole height twice.

### A tower standing on a building
Same picture, other way round. You know the building, or you know the tower; the two angles come from the same point.

Building 20 m seen at $30^\circ$, tower top at $60^\circ$, both from one point:

- Ground: $d = 20\cot 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}$ m.
- Tower: $d(\tan 60^\circ - \tan 30^\circ) = 20\sqrt{3} \times \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = 40$ m.

> **Tip:** The building's triangle is $20 = d\tan 30^\circ$; the tower's is $20 + t = d\tan 60^\circ$. Two equations, two unknowns.

### Watching from a roof
From a building's roof you look **down** at a tower's foot and **up** at its top. Two angles, one roof.

- Depression $\alpha$ of the foot: $d = b\cot\alpha$ where $b$ is the building's height.
- Elevation $\beta$ of the top: tower $= b + d\tan\beta$.

Building 10 m, depression $30^\circ$, elevation $60^\circ$: $d = 10\sqrt{3}$ m and tower $= 10 + 10\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3} = 40$ m.

> **Watch:** The building's height is inside the second triangle too. Forgetting the extra $b$ is the most common slip here.

### The broken tree
A tree breaks and the top touches the ground some distance away, making angle $\theta$ with the ground.

Let $x$ be the distance from the foot to the touching point:

- Standing stump $= x\tan\theta$.
- Broken piece (the slanting hypotenuse) $= x\sec\theta = \dfrac{x}{\cos\theta}$.
- Original height $=$ stump $+$ broken piece.

At $x = 15$ m and $\theta = 30^\circ$: stump $= 5\sqrt{3}$ m, broken piece $= \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{3}/2} = 10\sqrt{3}$ m, total $= 15\sqrt{3}$ m.

> **Example:** A quick check: the broken piece must be longer than the stump, because it is the slanting side.

### A slipping ladder
A ladder of fixed length $L$ rests at angle $\theta_1$, then slips to $\theta_2$. Both positions share $L$:

- Foot slides by $L\cos\theta_2 - L\cos\theta_1$ (the new angle is smaller, so its cosine is bigger).
- Top drops by $L\sin\theta_1 - L\sin\theta_2$.

Ladder 10 m from $60^\circ$ to $30^\circ$: the foot moves $10\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 10\times\dfrac{1}{2} = 5\sqrt{3} - 5 = 5(\sqrt{3}-1)$ m.

> **Tip:** Length stays constant. That single fact links the two triangles.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: One angle (30°, 45° or 60°) is given with the height or the distance.
pyqPatterns.approach:
45°: distance = height.
30°: distance = height × √3. 60°: distance = height ÷ √3.

example.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 20 m tower is 30°. How far is the point from the base?
example.solution:
30° rule: distance = height × √3
Distance = 20 × √3
So the point is **20√3 m** away

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A lighthouse, cliff or plane looks down at a ship, car or building.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Depression from the top = elevation from the object.
Then use the same 45° / 30° / 60° rules.

example.q: From a 100 m cliff, a boat is seen at a depression of 30°. How far is the boat from the cliff base?
example.solution:
Depression 30° from top = elevation 30° from the boat
30° rule: distance = height × √3
Distance = 100 × √3 = **100√3 m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: You walk closer (or two people stand apart) and the angle changes, e.g. 30° to 60°.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Call the height h and write each distance in terms of h.
The difference of the two distances is the distance walked.

example.q: Walking 40 m towards a tower, the elevation changes from 30° to 60°. Find the height.
example.solution:
Far spot: h × √3. Near spot: h ÷ √3
Gap = h × √3 − h ÷ √3 = 2h ÷ √3
2h ÷ √3 = 40, so h = 40 × √3 ÷ 2
Height = **20√3 m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A car or boat moves at a steady speed and the angle changes after some time.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Distance moved = speed × time.
Then treat it like a two-angle problem.

example.q: A car moves at 6 m/s. The angle of depression of it from a tower changes from 30° to 60° in 6 s. Find the tower's height.
example.solution:
Distance moved = 6 × 6 = 36 m
Far − near = h × √3 − h ÷ √3 = 2h ÷ √3
2h ÷ √3 = 36, so h = 36 × √3 ÷ 2
Height = **18√3 m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A statue on a pedestal, or a flagstaff on a tower, seen at two angles from one point.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Find the full height and the lower part separately.
Subtract to get the top part.

example.q: A statue stands on a 30 m pedestal. From a point, the pedestal top is at 45° and the statue top at 60°. Find the statue's height.
example.solution:
45° on the pedestal top → distance = 30 m
Full height at 60° = 30 × √3
Statue = 30√3 − 30 = **30(√3 − 1) m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A shadow length is given for one object, and you need the height of another.
pyqPatterns.approach:
At the same time, height and shadow grow in the same ratio.
Set up a simple proportion.

example.q: A 1.5 m stick casts a 2.5 m shadow. At the same time a tower casts a 75 m shadow. Find the tower's height.
example.solution:
Shadow grows from 2.5 to 75, which is 30 times
Height grows 30 times too
1.5 × 30 = **45 m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A tree breaks and its top touches the ground at some distance, making an angle.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Standing part + broken part = original height.
Use the 30-60-90 triangle to get both parts.

example.q: A tree breaks and its top touches the ground 15 m from the base, making 30° with the ground. Find the original height.
example.solution:
Standing part is opposite 30°, so it is half the broken part
Base 15 = standing × √3, so standing = 15 ÷ √3 = 5√3
Broken part = 2 × 5√3 = 10√3
Total = 5√3 + 10√3 = **15√3 m**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The slanting length (ladder, wire, thread) is given with its angle.
pyqPatterns.approach:
Use the 30-60-90 triangle: sides are in the ratio 1 : √3 : 2.
The slanting length is the "2".

example.q: A 60 m cable makes 60° with the ground. How tall is the pole?
example.solution:
Sides are in ratio 1 : √3 : 2
Cable (2 parts) = 60, so 1 part = 30
Pole is opposite 60° = √3 parts = 30 × √3 = **30√3 m**

solvedExamples.shortcut: At $45^\circ$, distance = height — no calculation at all. (Diagram: eye at the point, horizontal to the tower, angle up to the top.)

solvedExamples.q: The shadow of a tower is $40\sqrt{3}$ m long when the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 30° → height = $\frac{\text{shadow}}{\sqrt3}=\frac{40\sqrt3}{\sqrt3}=40$ m. The $\sqrt3$ cancels by design.

solvedExamples.q: From the top of a 100 m high cliff, the angle of depression of a ship is $30^\circ$. Find the distance of the ship from the base of the cliff.
solvedExamples.solution:
Depression $30^\circ$ = elevation $30^\circ$ at the ship. $\tan30^\circ=\frac{100}{d}$

$\frac{1}{\sqrt3}=\frac{100}{d}\Rightarrow d=100\sqrt3$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Flip depression to elevation, then the 30° rule: $d=\sqrt3\times100=100\sqrt3$ m. Trap: $\frac{100}{\sqrt3}$ (that is the 60° answer).

solvedExamples.q: Walking 40 m towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. Find the height of the tower.
solvedExamples.solution:
Let $h$ be the height and $x$ the nearer distance. Then $x\tan60^\circ=h$ and $(x+40)\tan30^\circ=h$:

$h\cot60^\circ+40=h\cot30^\circ\Rightarrow40=h(\sqrt3-\frac{1}{\sqrt3})=\frac{2h}{\sqrt3}\Rightarrow h=20\sqrt3$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Direct formula: $h=\frac{d}{\cot30-\cot60}=\frac{40\sqrt3}{2}=20\sqrt3$ m. For a 30–60 pair the height is always $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$ of the walked distance.

solvedExamples.q: A statue stands on a 30 m high pedestal. From a point on the ground, the angle of elevation of the top of the pedestal is $45^\circ$ and that of the top of the statue is $60^\circ$. Find the height of the statue.
solvedExamples.solution:
From the $45^\circ$ observation: $d=\frac{30}{\tan45^\circ}=30$ m.

From the $60^\circ$ observation: $30+\text{statue}=30\tan60^\circ=30\sqrt3$.

So statue $=30\sqrt3-30=30(\sqrt3-1)$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 45° fixes $d$ = pedestal height; statue $=d(\tan60-\tan45)=30(\sqrt3-1)$. Keep the factored surd — that is how the options read.

practice.q: A vertical pole 12 m high casts a shadow on level ground when the sun's elevation is $45^\circ$. The length of the shadow is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → shadow = height = 12 m.

practice.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a 30 m high tower from a point on the ground is $60^\circ$. The distance of the point from the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → distance $=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m. Trap: $30\sqrt3$ (that is the 30° rule).

practice.q: From the top of a 60 m high lighthouse, the angle of depression of a boat is $60^\circ$. The horizontal distance of the boat from the lighthouse is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → $d=\frac{h}{\sqrt3}=20\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: If the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$ and a tower's shadow is $30\sqrt{3}$ m long, the height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30° → height = shadow ÷ $\sqrt3$ = 30 m.

practice.q: A ladder 20 m long leans against a wall at $45^\circ$ to the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
practice.shortcut: Ladder is the hypotenuse: $h=L\sin\theta$. At 45°: $h=\frac{L}{\sqrt2}$. Trap: 10 is the $\frac{L}{2}$ guess.

practice.q: Two men stand on opposite sides of a tower, 80 m apart, and observe its top at elevations of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Opposite sides → add the cotangents: $\frac{80}{\frac{4}{\sqrt3}}=20\sqrt3$ m. Trap: subtracting gives $\frac{80\sqrt3}{2}=40\sqrt3$ (wrong side of the figure).

practice.q: On walking 20 m towards a tower the angle of elevation of its top rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30–60 pair: $h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times d=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times20=10\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: The shadow of a pole is $\sqrt{3}$ times the height of the pole. The angle of elevation of the sun is:
practice.shortcut: Shadow $\sqrt3\times$ height is the signature of 30° ($d=\sqrt3h$). Trap: 60° inverts the ratio.

practice.q: From the top of a 60 m high lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships on the same side are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The distance between the ships is:
practice.solution:
Distances from the base: far $=60\cot30^\circ=60\sqrt3$, near $=60\cot60^\circ=\frac{60}{\sqrt3}=20\sqrt3$.

Gap $=60\sqrt3-20\sqrt3=40\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Gap $=h(\cot30-\cot60)=60\cdot\frac2{\sqrt3}=40\sqrt3$ m — same $\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times$ nothing; here $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3}$. Watch: far minus near, never add.

practice.q: From a point 20$\sqrt{3}$ m from the base of a building, the elevation of the top of the building is $30^\circ$ and of the top of the tower standing on it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution:
Building: $h_b=20\sqrt3\tan30^\circ=20$ m.

Building + tower: $20\sqrt3\tan60^\circ=60$ m. Tower $=60-20=40$ m.
practice.shortcut: $\text{tower}=d(\tan60-\tan30)=20\sqrt3(\sqrt3-\frac1{\sqrt3})=20\sqrt3\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt3}=40$ m.

practice.q: A tree breaks due to a storm and the broken part touches the ground 15 m from the base, making an angle of $30^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the tree before breaking was:
practice.solution:
Fallen part $=\frac{15}{\cos30^\circ}=\frac{30}{\sqrt3}=10\sqrt3$ m; standing part $=15\tan30^\circ=5\sqrt3$ m.

Total $=15\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Tree $=\frac{b}{\cos\theta}+b\tan\theta=10\sqrt3+5\sqrt3=15\sqrt3$. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ (forgotten standing part).

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the tops of two towers from the midpoint of the line joining their bases are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. If the towers are 60 m apart, the difference of their heights is:
practice.solution:
Each base is 30 m from the midpoint.

$h_1=30\tan30^\circ=10\sqrt3$, $h_2=30\tan60^\circ=30\sqrt3$. Difference $=20\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Midpoint splits 60 into 30 + 30; heights are $30\times\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ and $30\times\sqrt3$ → difference $20\sqrt3$ m. (Ratio check: heights are always 1 : 3 here.)

practice.q: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ while the car approaches uniformly at 6 m/s for 6 seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Speed × time gives the walked distance; then the 30–60 pair: $h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\times36=18\sqrt3$ m.

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points 40 m apart on the same side of it are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{40}{\sqrt3-1}$ → multiply by $\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3+1}$ → $20(\sqrt3+1)$ m. The $30/45$ pair always ends in $(\sqrt3+1)\times\frac{d}{2}$.

practice.q: From the roof of a 7 m high building, the angle of elevation of the top of a tower is $60^\circ$ and the angle of depression of its base is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution:
Depression $45^\circ$: horizontal distance $d=\frac{7}{\tan45^\circ}=7$ m.

Elevation $60^\circ$: top above roof $=7\tan60^\circ=7\sqrt3$.

Tower $=7+7\sqrt3=7(1+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: 45° depression gives $d$ = building height (7); tower $=7+7\sqrt3$. Add the building back — the top angle only measures the part above the roof.

practice.q: A kite is flying with $30^\circ$ elevation from a point on level ground. If the kite's thread (assumed straight) is $100$ m long, the kite's height above the ground is:
practice.shortcut: Hypotenuse × sin. Trap: $50\sqrt3$ — that uses cos.

practice.q: From a $20$ m high tower, the angle of depression of a car on level ground is $45^\circ$. The car's distance from the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → distance = height. Trap: $20\sqrt3$ — that is the 30° rule.

practice.q: A cable of length $60$ m runs from the top of a pole to the ground, making $60^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the pole is:
practice.shortcut: Hypotenuse × sin60. Trap: $60\sqrt3$ — forgetting to halve.

practice.q: A vertical stick $1.5$ m long casts a shadow $2.5$ m long. At the same time, a nearby tower casts a shadow $75$ m long. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Ratio trick: height = shadow × (stick/shadow-stick) = $75 × 0.6$.

practice.q: A ladder of length $30$ m leans against a wall at $60^\circ$ to the ground. The foot of the ladder is at what distance from the wall?
practice.shortcut: Cos for the ground leg. Trap: $15\sqrt3$ — that is the wall height side.

practice.q: From the top of a cliff $80$ m high, the angle of depression of a ship is $45^\circ$. The distance of the ship from the foot of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: 45° flip → distance = height.

practice.q: A straight wire from the top of a $50$ m tower reaches the ground $50$ m from the base. The angle the wire makes with the ground is:
practice.solution: $\tan\theta = \frac{50}{50} = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 45^\circ$ (the wire length $50\sqrt2$ m is a distractor).
practice.shortcut: Height = ground distance → 45°. Trap: using the wire as if tangent asked for it.

practice.q: The shadow of a tower is $18$ m long when the sun's elevation is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 45° → shadow = height.

practice.q: From a point on the ground, the elevation of an aeroplane is $60^\circ$. If the plane is $1000$ m away along the line of sight, its height above the ground is:
practice.shortcut: Line of sight = hypotenuse: sin60. Trap: $1000\sqrt3$ (used tan60 on the hypotenuse).

practice.q: A pole $10$ m high casts a shadow $25$ m long. At the same moment, the shadow of a building is $90$ m. The building's height is:
practice.shortcut: $90 × \frac{10}{25} = 36$. Trap: $40$ — dividing 90 by the pole height ratio inverted.

practice.q: From a $\frac{80}{\sqrt{3}}$ m high tower, the angles of depression of two cars due north of it are $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The distance between the cars is:
practice.shortcut: Far minus near, both scaled by $h$. Trap: $\frac{160\sqrt3}{3}$ — a slipped surd.

practice.q: The angle of elevation of the top of a tower from a point $30\sqrt{3}$ m from its base is $30^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30° → distance is √3 × height; divide back.

practice.q: A tree casts a shadow $60$ m long when the sun's elevation is $30^\circ$. The height of the tree is:
practice.shortcut: 30°: height = shadow/√3 = $60/\sqrt3 = 20\sqrt3$. Trap: 20 — dividing twice.

practice.q: A pole casts a shadow equal to its own height. The sun's angle of elevation is:
practice.shortcut: Equal shadow and height is the 45° signature.

practice.q: From a point $15$ m from the base of a flagstaff, the elevation of its top is $60^\circ$. The height of the flagstaff is:
practice.shortcut: 60° → height = √3 × distance. Trap: $5\sqrt3$ — that is the distance rule inverted.

practice.q: A ladder $20$ m long rests against a wall at $30^\circ$ to the ground. The height it reaches on the wall is:
practice.shortcut: sin30 = ½ → half the ladder. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ — that is the foot distance ($20\cos30$).

practice.q: The elevation of a hilltop from a point $45$ m away (horizontal) is $60^\circ$. The hill's height is:
practice.shortcut: 60° multiplies the distance by √3.

practice.q: The value of $\tan^2 75^\circ + \tan^2 15^\circ$ is:
A $12$ m ladder leans at $45^\circ$ against a vertical wall. The height it reaches is:
practice.shortcut: 45°: height = $\frac{L}{\sqrt2} = 6\sqrt2$. Trap: 6 — that would be sin30.

practice.q: A tower subtends $75^\circ$ at a point $10$ m from its base (horizontal). Its height is:
practice.shortcut: $\tan75^\circ = 2+\sqrt3$ from the 45+30 identity. Keep it factored.

practice.q: The shadow of a tower is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ times its height. The sun's elevation is:
practice.shortcut: Short shadow means a HIGH sun: 60°. Trap: 30° — the reciprocal ratio.

practice.q: On walking $40$ m towards a tower, the angle of elevation of its top changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: 30–60 pair: $h = \frac{\sqrt3}{2} × 40$. Trap: $40\sqrt3$ — forgot the ½ factor.

practice.q: Two men stand on opposite sides of a tower, $40$ m apart. They observe the top at elevations $60^\circ$ and $30^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Opposite sides add: $\frac{D\sqrt3}{4}$. Trap: $20\sqrt3$ — same-side formula (subtracted).

practice.q: From the top of a $60$ m lighthouse, the angles of depression of two ships due east of it are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The distance between the ships is:
practice.shortcut: Gap $= h · \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = 40\sqrt3$. Trap: adding the distances.

practice.q: The elevations of the tops of two towers from the midpoint of the line joining their bases are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. If the towers are $60$ m apart, the difference of their heights is:
practice.shortcut: Heights at 30°/60° from equal bases are 1:3 → difference is $2 × 10\sqrt3$.

practice.q: Two poles of equal height stand at the two ends of a $30$ m segment. From the midpoint of the segment, the elevation of each top is $60^\circ$. The height of each pole is:
practice.solution: Midpoint is $15$ m from each base: $h = 15\tan60^\circ = 15\sqrt3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Equal angles at the midpoint ⇒ equal heights; one tangent finishes it. Trap: $15$ — dropping the multiplier.

practice.q: The angles of elevation of the top of a tower from two points $20$ m apart on the same side are $30^\circ$ and $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Rationalise $\frac{20}{\sqrt3-1}$ by multiplying $(\sqrt3+1)/(\sqrt3+1)$.

practice.q: Two men on opposite sides of a $50\sqrt{3}$ m high tower are $100$ m apart. The smaller of the two elevation angles of the top is:
practice.solution: $\cot\alpha + \cot\beta = \frac{100}{50\sqrt3} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}$. The 30–60 pair sums to $\frac{4}{\sqrt3}$ — too big; 45–60: $1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3} \approx 1.577 > 1.155$. Try 60–60: $\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ exactly. So both are $60^\circ$; the smaller is $60^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{D}{h} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3} = \cot60 + \cot60$ — symmetric case: both angles 60°.

practice.q: From a cliff, the depressions of two boats on the same side at distances $15\sqrt{3}$ m apart are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 15\sqrt3 \Rightarrow h = 22.5$ m. (Trust the algebra over pretty options.)

practice.q: Walking $50(\sqrt{3}-1)$ m towards a hill changes its elevation from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$. The height of the hill is:
practice.shortcut: The walk distance was engineered to cancel the denominator.

practice.q: Two observers on opposite sides of a tower are $40(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})$ m apart and see its top at $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: $h = \frac{40(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt3})}{1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}} = 40$ m... careful: $\cot45^\circ = 1$, $\cot60^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, sum $= 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ exactly, so $h = 40$ m.
practice.shortcut: The separation equals h × (sum of cots) — here the sum is exactly the given factor.

practice.q: From the top of a tower, the angle of depression of a car changes from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ while the car approaches uniformly at $6$ m/s for $6$ seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{vt\sqrt3}{2} = 18\sqrt3$. Trap: 36 — treating the walk as the height.

practice.q: A boat approaching a cliff at $5$ m/s sees the angle of depression of its top change from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ in $4$ seconds. The height of the cliff is:
practice.shortcut: Rationalise: $\frac{20(\sqrt3+1)}{2}$.

practice.q: A car moving at $4$ m/s takes $5$ seconds for the elevation of a tower's top to change from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{vt\sqrt3}{2}$ again — the 30–60 pair is worth memorising.

practice.q: From an $18\sqrt{3}$ m high tower, a car's depression grows from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as it approaches at $6$ m/s. The time (in seconds) it now takes to reach the base of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: Near distance $h\cot60$ over speed. Trap: $3\sqrt3$ — using the FAR distance.

practice.q: The elevation of a $10$ m pole's top changes from $45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as a cyclist approaches. The distance cycled is:
practice.shortcut: Far $h\cot45 = 10$, near $\frac{10}{\sqrt3}$; difference $10 - \frac{10}{\sqrt3}$.

practice.q: A man walking at $2$ m/s towards a tower finds the elevation changing from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in $9$ seconds. The height of the tower is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{18\sqrt3}{2} = 9\sqrt3$.

practice.q: A tower is $15\sqrt{3}$ m high. A car's depression angle from the top grows from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as the car approaches at $5$ m/s. The time for this change is:
practice.shortcut: Cot-gap distance ÷ speed. Trap: 2 s — halving instead of multiplying.

practice.q: Walking $3\sqrt{3}$ m towards a pole raises the elevation of its top from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The pole's height is:
practice.solution: $h = \frac{3\sqrt3 \cdot \sqrt3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}$ m... exact: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = 3\sqrt3 \Rightarrow h = \frac{9}{2} = 4.5$ m. With the closest clean option set, $h = 3\sqrt3/1.5$... recompute cleanly: $h = \frac{3\sqrt3 \times \sqrt3}{2} = \frac{9}{2}$ m.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2h}{\sqrt3} = vt$ with $vt = 3\sqrt3$ gives $h = \frac{9}{2}$ m — trust the algebra.

practice.q: From a tower of height $15$ m, a cyclist's depression grows from $45^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ as he rides at $3$ m/s. After the second sighting, the time to reach the tower base is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{h\cot60}{v} = \frac{5\sqrt3}{3}$ s. (Keep the surd exact.)

practice.q: A cyclist rides toward a $12\sqrt{3}$ m pole at $6$ m/s; the elevation of the pole top rises from $30^\circ$ to $60^\circ$. The cycling time for this change is:
practice.solution: Gap $= 12\sqrt3\cot30^\circ - 12\sqrt3\cot60^\circ = 36 - 12 = 24$ m; time $= \frac{24}{6} = 4$ s... exact: $\frac{24}{6} = 4$ s.
practice.shortcut: Cot-gap ÷ speed. Trap: 2 s — halving the gap.

practice.q: A boat moving at $4$ m/s holds a straight course toward a cliff; the elevation of its top rises from $30^\circ$ to $45^\circ$ over $10(\sqrt{3}+1)$ seconds. The cliff's height is:
practice.solution: Sailed: $4 \times 10(\sqrt3+1) = 40(\sqrt3+1)$ m $= h(\cot30\circ - \cot45\circ) = h(\sqrt3-1)$, so $h = \frac{40(\sqrt3+1)^2}{2} = 20(4+2\sqrt3) = 40(2+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: Rationalise by $(\sqrt3+1)$: the square gives $4+2\sqrt3$; factor out 2. Trap: $20(\sqrt3+1)$ — dropping the square.

practice.q: A train moving at $20$ m/s passes a signal post; the depression of a point on the track $2$ s later is $45^\circ$ from a $50$ m high signal bridge. How far is the train from the bridge base $2$ s after passing the post?
practice.solution: Covered $20 \times 2 = 40$ m; remaining to the bridge base $= 50\cot45^\circ = 50$ m.
practice.shortcut: Motion gives the distance; the cot gives what remains. Trap: 90 — adding instead of tracking remaining.

practice.q: A statue stands on a $30$ m high pedestal. From a point on the ground, the elevation of the top of the pedestal is $45^\circ$ and that of the top of the statue is $60^\circ$. The height of the statue is:
practice.shortcut: 45° fixes d = pedestal height. Trap: $30\sqrt3$ — that is the whole structure.

practice.q: From a point $20\sqrt{3}$ m from the base of a building, the elevation of the top of the building is $30^\circ$ and of the top of the tower standing on it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: Building $= 20\sqrt3\tan30^\circ = 20$ m; whole $= 20\sqrt3\tan60^\circ = 60$ m; tower $= 40$ m.

practice.q: From the roof of a $7$ m high building, the elevation of the top of a tower is $60^\circ$ and the depression of its base is $45^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
practice.solution: Depression 45°: $d = 7$ m. Above-roof part $= 7\tan60^\circ = 7\sqrt3$. Tower $= 7 + 7\sqrt3 = 7(1+\sqrt3)$ m.
practice.shortcut: Add the building back — the top angle only sees the part above the roof.

practice.q: A tree breaks due to a storm; the top touches the ground $15$ m from the base, making $30^\circ$ with the ground. The height of the tree before breaking was:
practice.shortcut: $b\tan\theta + \frac{b}{\cos\theta}$. Trap: $10\sqrt3$ — forgot the standing part.

practice.q: A flagstaff stands on a $10$ m high tower. From a point on the ground, the elevation of the tower top is $45^\circ$ and of the flagstaff top is $60^\circ$. The flagstaff's length is:
practice.shortcut: 45° below ⇒ d = 10; upper piece $= d(\tan60 - \tan45)$.

practice.q: The elevations of the bottom and the top of a $20$ m tall antenna on a building, from a point on the ground, are $45^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the building is:
practice.shortcut: Antenna $= d(\sqrt3 - 1)$; building $= d$; solve d from the antenna first. Trap: $10(\sqrt3+1)$ — that is the BUILDING.

practice.q: A $15\sqrt{3}$ m high pole breaks and the top touches the ground making $30^\circ$ with the ground. At what distance from the base does the top touch the ground?
practice.solution: Standing $= b\tan30^\circ = \frac{b}{\sqrt3}$; broken $= \frac{b}{\cos30^\circ} = \frac{2b}{\sqrt3}$. Sum $= \frac{3b}{\sqrt3} = b\sqrt3 = 15\sqrt3 \Rightarrow b = 15$ m.
practice.shortcut: $b\tan30 + \frac{b}{\cos30} = b\sqrt3$ when θ = 30° — solve for b.

practice.q: From the top of a cliff, the depressions of the top and the foot of a $9$ m tall lighthouse are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$. The height of the cliff is:
practice.solution: Let cliff $= H$, horizontal $= d$: $H - 9 = d\tan30^\circ$ and $H = d\tan60^\circ$. Subtract: $9 = d(\sqrt3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt3}) = \frac{2d}{\sqrt3} \Rightarrow d = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}$; $H = \frac{9\sqrt3}{2}\cdot\sqrt3 = 13.5$ m.
practice.shortcut: Two cot equations, subtract the lighthouse. Trap: $9\sqrt3$ — that is $H - 9$'s neighbour, not H.

practice.q: A bamboo $\sqrt{13}$ m high breaks; the top touches the ground $2$ m from the stem. The height of the break above the ground is:
practice.solution: Standing $a$, broken $\sqrt{13 - a^2} = 2$ (hypotenuse check: $a^2 + 2^2 = 13$) $\Rightarrow a^2 = 9 \Rightarrow a = 3$ m.
practice.shortcut: Pythagoras: standing$^2$ + touch distance$^2$ = original$^2$.
